title: Stars that never set, stars that never rise
subtitle: How your latitude sorts the sky into three zones

sections.heading: Three kinds of star
body: After this lesson you will be able to say, for any star, whether it is always up from where you live, sometimes up, or never up, using nothing but your latitude and the star's distance from the pole.

The sky turns around the celestial pole that is above your horizon. From {{place}} that is the {{pole}}, and it stands {{poleAltitude}} above the horizon, the same number as your latitude. Picture a circle around that pole that just touches the horizon below it. Its radius equals your latitude. Any star inside that circle turns around the pole without ever reaching the horizon. Such stars are called circumpolar: they are up all night, every night of the year, and in the daytime too, hidden by the bright sky.

There is a matching circle around the opposite pole, which lies the same number of degrees below your horizon on the other side. Stars inside it never climb above the horizon at all. Everything in between rises and sets. (On the equator both circles shrink to nothing, so every star rises and sets.)

steps.caption: Facing north on an October evening from mid-northern latitudes (41°N, the latitude of Chicago, Madrid or Beijing). The circle is 41° around the pole and just touches the horizon. The Little Dipper, Cassiopeia, Cepheus and Draco are inside it. The Big Dipper is at its lowest, skimming the rooftops.

Half an hour per second. Watch the end of the Dipper's handle: Alkaid slides along the horizon around midnight and comes back up without quite setting. From 41°N it sits right on the edge of the circle; from farther south it would dip below.

Capella, low in the northeast, is 44° from the pole: just outside the 41° circle. It does set, but for less than four hours out of every 24. Stars farther from the pole spend longer below the horizon.

Facing south in February with the ground switched off, so you can see below the horizon. This circle is the zone that never rises from 41°N. Canopus, the second-brightest star in the sky, passes about 4° under the horizon, straight below Sirius.

Now the southern version, from mid-southern latitudes (34°S, the latitude of Sydney, Cape Town or Santiago), facing south on a June evening. There is no bright pole star, but the 34° circle around the south celestial pole holds the Southern Cross, Alpha and Beta Centauri and both Magellanic Clouds: they never set there. The Big Dipper, in turn, never rises.

figures.caption: A side view of the sky along the north–south line. The celestial pole stands as high above the horizon as your latitude, so a cap of sky that size around it never sets, and a matching cap around the other pole never rises. Slide the latitude and watch both caps grow or vanish.

misconception.myth: The stars are only in the sky at night.
misconception.fact: Stars are above the horizon by day as often as by night; the bright daytime sky simply hides them. Circumpolar stars are up 24 hours a day, every day of the year.

thinkAbout.question: Where on Earth would every star you can see be circumpolar?
thinkAbout.answer: At the North or South Pole. There the celestial pole is straight overhead, so the never-sets cap is the whole visible half of the sky: no star rises or sets, they all circle parallel to the horizon. Drag the figure's latitude slider to 90° to see it.

sections.heading: What is circumpolar where you are
body: A star's distance from the pole is fixed, so you can sort stars by declination, the sky's version of latitude, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator. The rule is one subtraction: from latitude L, stars within 90° − L of the celestial equator rise and set; the rest never set (on your pole's side) or never rise (on the other side). From {{lat}} the never-set limit is a declination of {{circumpolarLimit}}. From 41°N it is +49°; from 34°S it is −56°.

From mid-northern latitudes (the US, Europe, Japan) the never-set group includes the Little Dipper ([[con:UMi|Ursa Minor]]), the W of [[con:Cas|Cassiopeia]], [[con:Cep|Cepheus]], [[con:Cam|Camelopardalis]] and nearly all of [[con:Dra|Draco]]. The Big Dipper qualifies from about 41°N and farther north. Its bowl is safely inside, but [[star:Alkaid|Alkaid]], the star at the tip of the handle, grazes the horizon at its lowest; in practice, when the Dipper is at the bottom of its circle (on October–November evenings), buildings and haze hide it. From mid-southern latitudes (Australia, South Africa, Argentina) the never-set group is the [[con:Cru|Southern Cross]], [[star:Rigil Kentaurus|Alpha]] and [[star:Hadar|Beta Centauri]] and the Magellanic Clouds.

Each group is the other hemisphere's never-rise group. The Southern Cross, Alpha Centauri, [[star:Canopus|Canopus]] and the Magellanic Clouds never rise from most of Europe and the northern US; the Little Dipper and most of the Big Dipper never rise from southern Australia. To see the other pole's stars you have to travel toward the equator or beyond it.

figures.caption: Everything inside the dashed circle never sets from your latitude; the circle's radius equals your latitude, so it just touches the horizon. Play the year: the figures inside only swing around the pole, while those outside dip below the horizon for part of the night.

check.prompt: From latitude 35° N, is Capella (declination +46°) circumpolar?
choices: Yes: it is north of the celestial equator
No: it would need a declination above +55°
Yes: every star above +35° never sets
Only in the months when it is up in the evening
check.explanation: The never-sets limit is 90° minus the latitude, +55° here. Capella, at +46°, dips about 9° below the northern horizon once a day.

sections.heading: The in-between stars are the seasonal ones
body: Most of the sky lies between the two circles. These stars rise and set, and the farther a star is from your visible pole, the lower and shorter its arc. From mid-northern latitudes, [[star:Vega|Vega]], well to the north, is above the horizon for about 18 hours out of 24, while [[star:Antares|Antares]], far to the south, manages only about 9 and never gets higher than two and a half fists. From mid-southern latitudes the roles swap: Antares passes almost overhead and Vega skims the northern horizon.

Because these stars spend part of each day below the horizon, whether you can see one depends on whether its time above the horizon falls at night. That changes through the year, which is why Orion is an evening sight in December–February and Scorpius in June–August, in both hemispheres. The circumpolar stars have no season. They only change position: from mid-northern latitudes the Dipper is high on March–May evenings and low on September–November ones.

steps.caption: Drag the latitude slider and watch Polaris. Go north and the pole climbs, so the never-set circle grows; at the North Pole it covers the whole visible sky. Go south to the equator and the pole drops to the horizon: nothing is circumpolar and every star rises and sets.

sections.tryIt: Find a circumpolar pattern tonight (Cassiopeia's W from mid-northern latitudes, the Southern Cross from mid-southern ones), then find it again at the same time in three months. It will be in a different part of its circle around the pole, but it will be there. Try the same with Orion and one of those two nights it will be missing.

figures.caption: Follow one star at a time. Each star's daily circle is seen edge-on as a line; the solid part is above the horizon. Compare Vega with Antares: the farther a star is from the visible pole, the shorter and lower its time above the horizon.

check.prompt: How many hours a day is a star on the celestial equator above the horizon, seen from anywhere but the poles?
choices: 12 hours, at any latitude
18 hours
6 hours
It depends on the month
check.explanation: Every horizon cuts the celestial equator exactly in half, so a star on it is up for 12 hours and down for 12. Stars on the pole's side of the equator are up longer, the others shorter.

keyPoints: The pole's height above the horizon equals your latitude: {{poleAltitude}} from {{place}}.
Stars closer to your visible pole than your latitude never set; stars that close to the other pole never rise.

Circumpolar from mid-northern latitudes: the Little Dipper, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, Draco, Camelopardalis and (barely) the Big Dipper. From mid-southern latitudes: the Southern Cross, Alpha and Beta Centauri and the Magellanic Clouds.
Everything in between rises and sets, and is seen at night only in its season.

questions.prompt: From latitude 40°N, which stars never set?
choices: Those within 40° of the north celestial pole
Those within 50° of the north celestial pole
Those within 40° of the celestial equator
Only Polaris
questions.explanation: The circumpolar circle has a radius equal to your latitude, because the pole stands that many degrees above the northern horizon.

questions.prompt: Why can you never see the Southern Cross from mid-northern latitudes such as Chicago, Rome or Beijing (about 42°N)?
choices: It is too faint for city skies
It is only up during the daytime
It is hidden behind the Milky Way
It lies within 42° of the south celestial pole, so it never rises
questions.explanation: Stars closer than your latitude to the opposite pole stay below the horizon all day and all year. The Cross is about 30° from the south celestial pole.

questions.prompt: You move from latitude 40°N to Anchorage, Alaska (latitude 61° north). What happens to the circumpolar region?
choices: It shrinks, because the pole is lower
It grows, because the pole is higher
It stays the same size but moves south
It disappears
questions.explanation: The never-set circle has a radius equal to your latitude. At 61° north many more stars, including Vega and Capella, never set.

questions.prompt: Cassiopeia is circumpolar from London (51°N). What does that tell you about seeing it from London in July?
choices: It is below the horizon in July
It is visible only before dawn
It is up all night; only its position around Polaris differs
It can be seen only from a dark site
questions.explanation: Circumpolar constellations are above the horizon at every hour of every night. The season changes where they sit around the pole, not whether they are up.

questions.prompt: From the equator (latitude 0°), how much of the sky is circumpolar?
choices: All of it
The northern half
A circle 23.4° across
None of it
questions.explanation: At the equator both poles lie on the horizon, so the never-set circle has zero radius: every star rises and sets.
